title: How to Register an Industrial Design in India Under the Designs Act, 2000
seo_title: Registering a Design in India: Designs Act 2000 Guide
meta_description: How to register an industrial design in India under the Designs Act, 2000: the novelty test, government fees, timeline and what can cancel it later.
format: step-by-step process with timelines and fees where official
intro: A company gets exclusive rights over the visual appearance of a product in India by filing a design application with the Patent Office's Design Wing in Kolkata under the Designs Act, 2000, and getting it registered. The shape, configuration, pattern, ornamentation or combination of lines and colour applied to the article has to be new or original, and it has to appeal to the eye of the person buying or using the article rather than to any function it performs. Registration takes effect from the date of filing, runs for ten years, and can be renewed once for a further five.

This matters most for a foreign manufacturer whose product is about to be sold, exhibited or licensed in India, and for an Indian company that has commissioned a distinctive look for a product from a vendor or design house and wants to stop a competitor from copying it. The filing has to happen before the design is shown anywhere in the world, because disclosure anywhere destroys the novelty the Act demands. As on 20 November 2026, the governing statute is the Designs Act, 2000 and the Designs Rules, 2001 as amended in 2021; nothing in the recent Budget cycles has replaced either.

sections.heading: What the Act will register, and what it will not
paragraphs: Section 2(d) of the Act defines a design as the visual features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colour applied to an article, in two or three dimensions, by an industrial process, judged solely by the eye in the finished article. A new phone case, a bottle, a chair, a tread pattern on a tyre or the layout of icons on a dashboard can all qualify if the look is distinctive and was created by or for the applicant.

The Act keeps three things out deliberately. A trademark stays with trademark law, because a mark tells a buyer who made the product rather than what it looks like. A property mark under the criminal law (now Section 345 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, after the Indian Penal Code was replaced from 1 July 2024) stays out for the same reason. An artistic work under Section 2(c) of the Copyright Act, such as a painting, a drawing or a photograph treated as art rather than as the look of a mass produced article, stays with copyright. A mere mechanical device, or a feature that exists only because of how the article has to work rather than how it looks, is excluded too; a hinge shaped only to let a lid close is not a design, even if no one else has made it that way before.

Getting this classification wrong is the most common reason an application stalls at the examination stage. A client who describes a product's packaging as a logo problem, when the actual asset worth protecting is the bottle's silhouette, ends up filing in the wrong registry and losing time while the product is already on shelves.

sections.heading: The novelty test is global, not local
paragraphs: Section 4 bars registration on four grounds: the design is not new or original, it was disclosed to the public anywhere in India or in any other country before the filing or priority date, it is not significantly distinguishable from designs already known, or it contains scandalous or obscene matter. The second ground is the one that catches people off guard, because it is not limited to India. A product shown at an overseas trade fair, published in an overseas catalogue, or sold in another country before the Indian application is filed can defeat novelty even though nothing happened in India.

The third ground, significant distinguishability, is judged by what courts call the eye test or ocular impression: does the finished article, taken as a whole, look different enough from what is already on the register or in the market, even if some individual features were already known separately. A design is not thrown out merely because a similar curve or a similar pattern existed before; the comparison is of the whole appearance.

Before filing, it is worth searching the Register of Designs on the IP India portal and the WIPO Global Design Database for anything close, because an examiner will raise the same prior art during examination and a contested registration can be cancelled years later on the same ground.

sections.heading: Filing, classification and examination
paragraphs: Applications are filed in the prescribed form with representations of the design (drawings or photographs showing every view needed to understand the shape), a statement of novelty, and the class of goods under the Locarno Classification, the international system administered by WIPO that groups articles by what they are used for rather than by industry. A single application can usually cover only one class, so a company with a range of products across different articles files separately for each class even if the visual theme is the same.

The application goes to the Design Wing in Kolkata, which is the only office that examines and prosecutes design applications in India even though applications can be filed at any of the patent office's branch locations or electronically through the IP India portal. An examiner checks the application for formal compliance and for the Section 4 grounds, and raises objections by way of an examination report if the application needs clarification, a narrower statement of novelty, or evidence that the article is not already known.

Filing electronically through the portal costs less than a physical filing of the same application, and an applicant or its agent can track the status of the application and respond to objections through the same portal. Once the objections are cleared, the design is registered and a certificate issued, with the registration dated back to the date of filing rather than the date of grant.

sections.heading: What it costs, and who pays less
paragraphs: The First Schedule to the Designs Rules, 2001, as amended in 2021, sets the official fee at a lower rate for a natural person, a Startup India recognised startup or an MSME registered small entity, and a higher rate for every other applicant, including a foreign company that is not a recognised Indian startup or small entity. A startup or small entity claiming the lower fee has to file Form-24 along with a current DPIIT recognition certificate or Udyam registration at the time of filing; without it, the higher fee applies and is not refunded later if the certificate surfaces afterwards.

If a reduced fee application is later assigned to an entity that does not qualify for the concession, the difference in fee becomes payable before the transfer is recorded. Renewal for the additional five year term, and restoration of a design that has lapsed for non payment of the renewal fee within the time allowed, both attract separate fees under the same schedule, again at two tiers depending on who is applying. A foreign applicant usually files through an Indian patent agent, since the Act requires an address for service in India and most foreign owners prefer a resident agent to handle office communications and renewal deadlines in any event.

sections.heading: How a registered design is attacked, and how it defends itself
paragraphs: Section 19 lets any interested person, at any time after registration, file a petition to cancel it on the grounds that the design was already registered or published in India or elsewhere before the priority date, is not new or original, is not registrable under the Act, or is not significantly distinguishable from a known design. A competitor who gets sued for copying very often answers by filing, or threatening to file, a Section 19 cancellation rather than only defending the suit.

Section 22 covers piracy, meaning the unauthorised application of a registered design, or an obvious imitation of it, to an article for sale, without the registered owner's consent. Section 22(3) makes every ground available for cancellation under Section 19 available as a defence in a piracy suit, so a defendant sued for copying can raise the same novelty or prior publication arguments inside the infringement case itself rather than filing a separate cancellation petition.

Where that defence is raised and the court records that it goes to the validity of the registration, Section 22(4) requires the suit or proceeding to be moved to a High Court. In S.D. Containers Indore v. Mold Tek Packaging Ltd (2020 INSC 668), the Supreme Court held that the expression High Court in Section 22(4) includes a High Court that does not have ordinary original civil jurisdiction, and that the transfer is tied to where the cause of action actually arose rather than simply to the registered owner's choice of forum. A plaintiff who files in the wrong city risks the suit being sent somewhere else entirely once a validity defence is raised.

sections.heading: Where design protection ends and copyright or trademark protection begins
paragraphs: Once an article's appearance is capable of being registered as a design under the Act, courts have treated the overlapping copyright in the underlying drawing as running out once the article has been reproduced more than fifty times by an industrial process, whether or not the owner actually registered the design. The practical effect is that a company cannot sit on an unregistered but industrially applied design and sue under copyright law indefinitely once mass production has started; registering the design, and renewing it, is the only way to keep an enforceable monopoly on the look of a mass produced article for the full period the law allows.

A logo, a brand name or get up that signals origin rather than appearance is better protected as a trademark, which can in principle last forever with renewal and does not depend on registering every variant of a product's shape. Many companies file both: a design registration for the product's physical form and a trademark for the name, logo or distinctive packaging get up that goes on it, because the two rights protect different things and expire on different clocks.

faqs.q: Can I register a design in India if I already registered the same product abroad?
faqs.a: You can apply, but a prior foreign registration or any prior publication of the design anywhere in the world before the Indian filing date can be used to argue that it is not new under Section 4(b). Some sources read a prior foreign registration as conclusive proof of publication; file in India before or at the same time as the first foreign filing rather than after.

faqs.q: How long does design registration actually take in India?
faqs.a: There is no statutory deadline for the Design Wing to decide an application, and practitioners report anywhere from under a year to close to two years depending on whether objections are raised and how quickly they are answered. An application that draws no examination objections is generally faster than one that needs the statement of novelty redrafted or prior art distinguished.

faqs.q: Does a design registration stop someone from copying the function of my product?
faqs.a: No. The Act protects only how an article looks, judged by the eye, not how it works. A competitor who builds a product that performs the same function but looks different has not committed design piracy, and a feature that exists only because of a mechanical necessity is excluded from registration in the first place.

faqs.q: Who can file a cancellation petition against my registered design?
faqs.a: Section 19 allows any person interested, which generally means a person who has a real commercial interest likely to be affected by the registration, such as a competitor in the same line of goods. A cancellation petition can be filed at any time after registration, so a registration is never entirely beyond challenge even years after it is granted.

faqs.q: Can a startup or small company pay a lower fee to register a design?
faqs.a: Yes. A natural person, a DPIIT recognised startup or an MSME registered small entity pays a lower fee under the First Schedule to the Designs Rules than any other applicant, provided Form-24 with the relevant certificate is filed along with the application. Without that certificate at filing, the full fee applies.
